cases.question: Our Singapore private company has one director. Can that sole director also act as company secretary, and what should we do when appointing a secretary? Please cite the official requirements. No accounting entry is requested.
cases.answer:
# Answer

Every company must have at least one company director and one company secretary. [ACRA: Step 4.3: Choosing company directors & other key officers | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority](https://www.acra.gov.sg/register/business/registering-different-business-structures/local-company/appointing-company-directors-other-key-officers/)

The company secretary must not be the same person as the sole director. [ACRA: Step 4.3: Choosing company directors & other key officers | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority](https://www.acra.gov.sg/register/business/registering-different-business-structures/local-company/appointing-company-directors-other-key-officers/)

A company secretary must be a real person (not a company), and must be a Singapore citizen, Singapore permanent resident, or someone who meets local residency rules. [ACRA: Step 4.3: Choosing company directors & other key officers | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority](https://www.acra.gov.sg/register/business/registering-different-business-structures/local-company/appointing-company-directors-other-key-officers/)

Because your company has a sole director, that sole director cannot also act as the company secretary under ACRA rules. [ACRA: Step 4.3: Choosing company directors & other key officers | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority](https://www.acra.gov.sg/register/business/registering-different-business-structures/local-company/appointing-company-directors-other-key-officers/)

exploratoryPairedControl.question: Explain accrual accounting versus cash accounting for a small business with unpaid supplier invoices. Give a practical explanation.
exploratoryPairedControl.answer:
# Direct Answer

For a small business handling unpaid supplier invoices, accrual accounting requires recognizing expenses and liabilities when goods or services are received regardless of when cash changes hands, whereas cash accounting records expenses only when cash is actually paid out to the supplier.

# Explanation

- Under the accrual basis of accounting, transactions are recorded in the periods in which the economic events occur.
- Under the cash basis of accounting, revenues and expenses are tracked strictly based on the physical movement of cash.
- Because the supplier invoice is unpaid, no cash outflow has occurred, meaning the expense is omitted from the income statement and the liability is omitted from the balance sheet until the settlement payment is eventually made.
- Choosing between these methods affects how financial performance is portrayed.
- Accrual accounting provides a more comprehensive view of obligations and financial commitments by matching expenses to the period the related benefits were consumed, whereas cash accounting offers simplicity and tracks immediate liquidity but may distort profitability when significant bills remain unpaid.

# Accounting Treatment

- Under accrual frameworks such as SFRS(I), the accrual basis is mandatory for general-purpose financial reporting to ensure that liabilities and matching expenses are captured in the correct accounting period.

# Conditions and Important Notes

- The applicability of either method depends on statutory reporting requirements, entity size, and whether the business prepares general-purpose financial statements or simpler tax-only computations.

# Verification Note

A specific rate, deadline, calculation, legal requirement, or provision reference is not included because this answer path has not independently verified that claim.
